content:
You already know how to map an area and how to pull demographic figures. Those guides stop at the files. This one is about the packet you hand to other leaders: the map, the data brief, sourced local history, and notes from conversations with several local groups and neighboring churches.

A target area report does not choose the plant's ministry. It shows what you observed, what you think it might mean, and which decisions are still open. The Senior Pastor and the other leaders who share the work still set the priorities. Everyfield does not grade the area, score other churches, or decide whether you should plant.

---

## What the report is for

Use the report when leaders need one packet they can check together. An identified geographic area is one factor in setting a launch date. The report shows the work behind that area. It is not a form you must finish before a Core Group can meet, and it is not a gate on the way to Launch Sunday.

Keep three kinds of material, and do not blend them.

- Observations, with the source and the date.
- Interpretations, labeled as yours.
- Decisions still open, with the blank left blank.

Leave out an average target family. A median age or a common household size describes a table, not a person you should design the church around. Leave out grades for other churches. Treat them as possible partners. Leave out any count of believers drawn from Census profiles.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not invent a household that stands for the area. If a figure describes a tract or a city, say that. Do not turn it into a family portrait and then plan as if you had met that family.
</Callout>

---

## Attach the map and the demographic brief

Do not repeat the data steps here. Build the map with [Mapping Your Target Area](/wiki/discovery/mapping-your-target-area). Pull the figures with [Finding Demographic Data for Your Area](/wiki/discovery/finding-demographic-data-for-your-area). Attach both. Include the area names, geographic codes, boundary vintage, table IDs, periods, and margins of error.

The Census Bureau describes the American Community Survey as a nationwide sample survey of social, economic, housing, and demographic characteristics. Each published estimate has a margin of error. The estimates describe areas across a collection period, not one household, and a small gap between two estimates may not be a real difference. Carry the period and the margin of error with the figure.

The official 2020 Census questionnaire asks how many people were living or staying at the address, along with housing tenure, sex, age, Hispanic origin, race, and relationship. It does not ask religious affiliation. The Census Bureau's comparison page describes the 2020 Census as a shorter set of questions, such as age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, and owner or renter status. It describes the American Community Survey as covering topics not on that census, such as education, employment, internet access, and transportation. Religion is not in either list. Pew Research Center reports that the decennial census has never directly asked Americans about their religion, and notes that some older efforts gathered faith information by other means. Those efforts are not a current tract profile. Do not label households or tracts as believers or nonbelievers from these tables.

<Callout type="important">
Census pages and the 2020 questionnaire were checked on October 26, 2026. Before a leadership decision, confirm the current table, geography, and period with the U.S. Census Bureau. Archive contacts and local plans go out of date too.
</Callout>

---

## Add history and published local needs

A map shows the outline you chose. History tells you what that place used to mean, and only when you can name the source.

Start with the offices that keep the records. The National Archives publishes contact information for state archives and historical societies. That list was current as of April 2022, so confirm the phone number or email before you rely on it. The American Association for State and Local History is the association for people who preserve and interpret state and local history. Ask your state archive, a local historical society, or a public library what they would read first for this place. Save the title, the publisher, the date, and the sentence you are using.

For older population figures tied to census geography, IPUMS NHGIS offers summary tables and mapping files from 1790 onward, for states, counties, tracts, and blocks. Keep the year and the geography beside any historical count. Tract lines move. A 1990 tract and today's tract are not automatically the same place.

For needs a government has already written down, read the local Consolidated Plan if your city or county publishes one. HUD describes that plan as a way for states and local jurisdictions to assess affordable housing and community development needs and market conditions, and to name priorities for certain federal funding programs. Quote what the plan says, name the year, and stop. A city's funding priority is not your church's ministry decision.

<Callout type="tip">
If a history source describes who used to live on a block, label it as history. People there now may have arrived later. The source cannot tell you their faith, their welcome, or what they need from a new church.
</Callout>

---

## Talk with several local groups

Figures and plans still miss what people will say out loud. Plan conversations with several local groups, not one well-connected friend. Meeting community leaders, and running a community needs survey, are separate work. This report only needs notes you can stand behind.

Sit with people who see different parts of the area. A librarian, a clinic or nonprofit worker, a shop owner, someone from a neighborhood association, and pastors already serving there will not tell you the same story. You do not need a quota. You do need more than one circle. If every conversation runs through the same two people, write that down.

Make the note the day you talk.

- Date, place, and how you met.
- The person's name and role, and whether they spoke for themselves or for an organization.
- What you asked.
- What they said, as close to their words as you can honestly get.
- The conclusion you are tempted to draw, on a separate line.

A few voices are not the area. Three parents can tell you that weekday childcare is hard for them. They cannot tell you it is the main need of every household. Mark a repeated theme as a theme in your notes.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"The first to plead his case seems right, Until another comes and examines him."* — Proverbs 18:17 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Treat neighboring churches as partners

List churches and ministries that already serve the area. Record the name, the location, and what you actually learned from a visit, a service, or a conversation. Do not score them. Do not rank friendliness, strength, or whether they are in your way. You do not have the evidence, and this report is the wrong place to try.

Ask what they already do, where they see strain, and whether a partnership would help or would crowd work they already do. The Cape Town Commitment treats partnership in mission as shared submission to Christ, not as a way to protect your own group's preferences. Take that as a posture for the conversation. Do not turn it into a sentence about another church's faithfulness.

Keep people who already belong to a congregation separate from people who do not yet trust Christ. A full room of people who moved from the church down the road is not proof that the area has been reached. A smaller crowd there is not a failure for you to exploit.

Possible partnerships belong in the report as options leaders should consider. Sharing a food distribution another church already runs is one example. Asking about a joint prayer gathering is another. Neither is decided because you typed it.

---

## Separate what you know from what you might do

Read the packet in three passes. First, what did a source say? Second, what do you think it means? Third, what have leaders not decided?

| What you write | What you leave out |
|---|---|
| A fact: source, date, place, and the words or figure | Your recommendation |
| A reading, labeled as yours, including who disagrees | A claim that the whole area agrees |
| The question leaders still have to answer | A priority written as if it were settled |

Name the needs you heard and the partnerships worth a conversation. Then stop. Ministry priorities stay with leaders. A demographic focus can later become one of the church's distinctives, as [Defining Your Church Values](/wiki/discovery/defining-your-church-values) describes. This report does not choose that focus, and it does not turn a focus into a rule about who is welcome. Choosing how to respond is a later act of leadership and prayer.

---

## Leave a packet another leader can check

- [ ] Attach the map and the demographic brief, with geography, period, and margins of error.
- [ ] Attach history sources with titles, publishers, and dates.
- [ ] Attach conversation notes from several local groups, and name who you did not hear.
- [ ] List neighboring churches as possible partners, with no scores.
- [ ] List needs and partnership ideas as considerations, not decisions.
- [ ] List decisions still open, and who will bring them to the Senior Pastor and the other leaders.
- [ ] Remove any average family profile and any religious label taken from Census data.

If a section has no source, write that it is not yet known and name the question you still need to ask. An honest gap beats a paragraph no one can check.

rulings: Bryan ruled B17 = Option B: "Community-informed ministry report" (2026-10-26).
Wording: kept the title Writing a Target Area Report and did not use any other product name for this report.
Did not link unpublished articles on meeting community leaders or a community needs survey. Named those tasks in words only.
No minimum number of conversations, no score or grade for other churches, and no average household profile.
Ministry priorities stay with the Senior Pastor and the other leaders who share the work. The report lists needs and possible partnerships as considerations, not decisions.
Scripture is Proverbs 18:17 LSB, checked one verse at a time on read.lsbible.org on 2026-10-26, rather than repeating Proverbs 18:13 from the two data guides.
